title: Find employees who are duplicates by name (appear more than once).
shortTitle: Find employees who are duplicates by name (appear more than once)
topicTitle: Find employees who are duplicates by name

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding duplicates by a key means grouping the stream by that key and keeping only the groups whose size is greater than one. The idiomatic Java 8 approach is `Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getName, Collectors.counting())`, then filter the resulting map entries where the count exceeds one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR auditor at the National Bank of India suspects some employees were entered twice by mistake. She sorts all the name cards into piles, one pile per name, then looks for any pile with more than one card. Those names are the duplicates. Grouping into piles and keeping the tall piles is exactly the duplicate check.

**One line to remember:** Group by the key, count each group, and keep the keys whose count is greater than one.

sections.s2_technical:
The cleanest way to find duplicates is to count occurrences of each key. `Collectors.groupingBy` partitions the stream into a map where the key is the grouping value and the value is produced by a downstream collector. Using `Collectors.counting()` as the downstream gives a `Map<String, Long>` of name to how many times it appeared.

Once you have that map you stream its entries and filter `entry -> entry.getValue() > 1`, which keeps only names seen more than once. Mapping each surviving entry back to its key with `Map.Entry::getKey` and collecting yields the list of duplicate names. The whole thing is two stream passes: one to build the counts, one to filter them.

An alternative trick for detecting (not counting) duplicates in a single pass uses a `Set`: `Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(); stream.filter(e -> !seen.add(e.getName()))`. The `add` method returns false when the element was already present, so NOT add is true exactly for the second and later sightings. This is elegant but stateful, so it must only be used on a sequential stream, never a parallel one, because the shared set is not safe across threads.

A senior nuance: the grouping approach is preferred in production because it is stateless from the caller's perspective, works correctly in parallel, and the count is often useful information in itself (how many times each name repeated), whereas the set trick is a neat one-liner for a sequential interview answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is auditing its employee master after a messy data migration, and the auditor fears some people were entered more than once under the same name, which would corrupt payroll by paying them twice. We must find every name that appears more than once so the duplicates can be investigated and merged. This is exactly how a group-and-count duplicate check works — all records are grouped by name, each group is counted, and only names with a count above one are reported.

The code defines an `Employee` with id and name. A `DuplicateFinderService` exposes `duplicateNames(List<Employee>)` using groupingBy with counting then filtering counts above one. The runnable `Main` feeds a list where Rajesh appears twice and logs the duplicate names.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: E1 Rajesh, E2 Priya, E3 Rajesh, E4 Amit, E5 Priya.

Step 1: Pass one streams all five records and groups by name. Rajesh collects E1 and E3, Priya collects E2 and E5, Amit collects E4.

Step 2: The counting downstream turns each group into a count, producing the map Rajesh equals 2, Priya equals 2, Amit equals 1.

Step 3: Pass two streams the map entries. Rajesh has count 2, which is greater than one, so it is kept.

Step 4: Priya has count 2, greater than one, kept.

Step 5: Amit has count 1, not greater than one, dropped.

Step 6: The surviving entries are mapped to their keys, giving the duplicate names Rajesh and Priya.

```
Oct 30, 2026 11:20:08 AM com.bank.dup.service.DuplicateFinderService duplicateNames
INFO: Name counts: {Rajesh=2, Priya=2, Amit=1}
Oct 30, 2026 11:20:08 AM com.bank.dup.Main lambda$main$0
WARNING: Duplicate name found: Rajesh
Oct 30, 2026 11:20:08 AM com.bank.dup.Main lambda$main$0
WARNING: Duplicate name found: Priya
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [E1 Rajesh, E2 Priya, E3 Rajesh, E4 Amit, E5 Priya]
    │
    ▼
  stream().collect(groupingBy(name, counting()))
    │
    ▼
  Map<String,Long>: {Rajesh=2, Priya=2, Amit=1}
    │
    ▼
  entrySet().stream().filter(count > 1)
    ├─ Rajesh=2 → >1 ✓ → keep ─┐
    ├─ Priya=2  → >1 ✓ → keep ─┤
    └─ Amit=1   → >1 ✗ → drop  │
                               ▼
  .map(Entry::getKey).collect(toList())  →  [Rajesh, Priya]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicates by a key, I group the stream by that key and keep the groups that have more than one element. In Java 8 I collect with groupingBy on the name, using the counting downstream collector, which gives me a map of each name to how many times it appeared. Then I stream the map's entries, filter the ones whose count is greater than one, and map them back to the name, giving me exactly the list of duplicate names.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was an audit after a messy data migration. The auditor feared some employees had been entered twice under the same name, which would corrupt payroll by paying them twice, so I needed every name appearing more than once. The group-and-count approach gave both the duplicate names and, as a bonus, the exact repeat count, which the auditor used to prioritise which records to merge first.

A senior point I always mention is that there is a clever single-pass alternative using a set: you add each name to a set and keep the element only when add returns false, because add returns false when the value was already present, so NOT add is true for the second and later sightings. It is an elegant one-liner, but it is stateful and relies on a shared mutable set, so it must only be used on a sequential stream, never a parallel one, where the set is not thread safe. In production I prefer the grouping approach precisely because it is parallel-safe and the count itself is useful information.
